shipped_rows.title_o: Cognitive–Affective Styles Associated With Position on War

blind_target.title: The Language of Political Aggression
blind_target.evidence_quote:
We sought to conceptually replicate two studies of the role of linguistic style in

predicting war attitudes and behaviors, Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013), in

the U.S. Congressional context.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
We add to this area by replicating two

previous studies: Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013) in the context of a

legislative body. The present study hypothesized that legislators who support war measures

would be externally focused and less cognitively complex in their speeches, while opponents

of war measures would be internally focused. Speeches were obtained pertaining to the

decisions for the U.S. to take military action in Kosovo, Iraq, and Libya. While we found

mixed results depending on the circumstances of a speciﬁc conﬂict, we demonstrate how

automated language analysis can be combined with voting records to better understand

behavioral action, such as legislative decision.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The abstract explicitly frames the combined conceptual replications as mixed across conflicts; results and discussion report supported and unsupported hypotheses across samples.

prior_decision.quote:
We sought to conceptually replicate two studies of the role of linguistic style in

predicting war attitudes and behaviors, Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013), in

the U.S. Congressional context.
prior_decision.reason: The paper explicitly replicates both Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013), testing Matsumoto and Hwang (2013) through Hypotheses 1 and 3 across the congressional speech samples, so Matsumoto and Hwang (2013) is an omitted target that requires its own replication record with a mixed outcome.

luna_triage.reason: The paper explicitly says it conceptually replicates Matsumoto and Hwang (2013), then describes their finding about linguistic markers preceding aggressive acts and tests the same directional predictions on congressional speech/voting. The sole supplied shipped original is Abe (2012), so it does not represent this separate original work.
luna_triage.omission_quote: The current work is a more direct replication of Matsumoto and Hwang (2013) with the only substantive diﬀerence being the sample itself and the outcome measure (e.g., voting for war rather than actual acts of aggression).
luna_triage.identity_quote: Matsumoto and Hwang (2013) used speeches of world and political group leaders to more directly predict political aggression from language markers.
